extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of nineteenth-century literature / general literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of a Victorian-era philosophical essay-novel (Sartor Resartus by Thomas Carlyle), focusing on themes, narrative method, and rhetorical/imagistic techniques used to portray a troubled protagonist and cultural critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what thou canst work at
rubrics_metrics.description: “Know thyself; till it be translated into this partially possible one, Know what thou canst work at.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues that self-knowledge is best achieved through productive work: 'Our Works are the mirror wherein the spirit first sees its natural lineaments.' The passage counsels writers/thinkers to focus on demonstrable activity (works) as the true test of capability rather than vague inward reflection. Surrounding commentary contrasts vague capability with 'fixed indubitable Performance' and treats works as the means to make the self articulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted aphorism: 'The end of Man is an Action, and not a Thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes purely speculative nourishment for the soul (e.g., carrying Epictetus' Enchiridion as companion but finding 'the nourishment it yielded was trifling') and emphasizes that meaningful life and creative output require action. For practitioners, the implied standard is to convert reflection into concrete work rather than remaining in contemplative paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a true Book that will outlast material works
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wondrous indeed is the virtue of a true Book... Thou who art able to write a Book... thou too art a Conqueror and Victor; but of the true sort... thou too hast built what will outlast all marble and metal, and be a wonder-bringing City of the Mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle elevates the lasting cultural power of a genuinely great book above physical monuments or political conquest. The guidance encourages aiming for works of lasting spiritual/intellectual value: books as 'spiritual trees' producing perennial leaves (commentaries, systems). The passage serves as both valuation (durability and moral/spiritual conquest) and an exhortation to authors to aspire to works that transmit spirit across ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emblematical, fragmentary narration with sparse direct notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor's remark: the Professor's story is 'imparted emblematically, in dim multifarious tokens... with only some touch of direct historical notice sparingly interspersed: little light-islets in the world of haze!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage describes a narrative method: present a character and life through emblematic fragments, tokens, and scattered direct facts rather than continuous, straightforward biography. Guidance implied for writers: use emblematic details, indirect signs (e.g., street-advertisements, 'paper-bags') and occasional explicit notices to create an enigmatic, atmospheric portrait. The author warns this produces obscurity (a limit to clarity) but also a particular expressive effect; an anti-pattern would be over-clarifying or forcing conventional linear exposition that defeats the emblematic mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative Protest (the Everlasting No) as character development
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the 'EVERLASTING NO' and its effect: 'my whole ME stood up... and with emphasis recorded its Protest... It is from this hour that I incline to date my Spiritual New-birth, or Baphometic Fire-baptism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle presents indignation and defiance—an active protest against nihilism or spiritual exile—as a legitimate engine of spiritual rebirth and development. For depiction of inner transformation in fiction, the text endorses framing a decisive psychological protest or defiant self-assertion as the turning point that yields a new center of identity. Use of charged rhetorical language and symbolic naming (Everlasting No, Baphometic Fire-baptism) is part of dramatizing this metamorphosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke unity between observer and landscape; personify dwellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage: 'for always, of its own unity, the soul gives unity to whatsoever it looks on with love; thus does the little Dwelling-place of men, in itself a congeries of houses and huts, become for us an individual, almost a person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique for writing evocative natural or urban description: render places as unified, almost-personal entities by projecting the observer's feeling of love or memory onto them. Use personification and unity-building metaphors so a town or landscape becomes an 'individual' in the reader's mind. This is a prescriptive image-making device for imbuing setting with emotional significance (anti-pattern: treating locale as mere backdrop without subjective relation).
